title: Staying fit to play trumpet and the warm-up routine
summary: Armstrong talks about quitting at 35, caring for stomach and lips, physical condition, and his warm-up. The talk turns to Dixieland, with a commercial break.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone

I think maybe now that I've passed the age when all trumpet players should quit, you know, you should quit playing once you're 35. No, that ain't well. Well, I've passed it too. Quit playing when you can't blow the ball. Well, I mean, you quit working after 35 and you enjoy it from there on in. You understand, you take care of your temperature. Oh, yeah. And then your stomach. Because your stomach ain't in good condition. You're bound to have fever blisters and hindrance, cold soles. You understand? So you know what to do with the horn. You have your technique and everything like that. And all you gotta do is sit back and relax and play. Good music. And it's just as hot as anything you would. You know, that's another thing. I always felt that you have to be in physical condition like an athlete to really play well. I used to be so close to that horn. I mean, I felt that horn was part of me for years. And if my finger hurt, I knew it when I was playing the horn. If I had a headache or something, it affected the style. And it just wasn't there. But boy, when you can plant your feet on the floor, your body's there 100% and you play it, you can be the master. You get that ring in your tone. That's where my point come in. Make all your days the same. And you have to do something about it. Because the Lord will help the poor, but not the poor lazy.
